Battery chemistry for electric vehicles (EVs) has evolved through several generations: (1) lead-acid (largely obsolete for traction applications), (2) nickel-metal hydride (NiMH, still used in some hybrid vehicles), (3) lithium-ion (Li-ion, the current standard), and (4) solid-state (under development, with anticipated commercialization by 2027-2030). Li-ion cells are further subdivided by cathode composition: NMC (nickel manganese cobalt), LFP (lithium iron phosphate), and NCA (nickel cobalt aluminum). Energy density ranges from approximately 150 Wh/kg (LFP) to 260 Wh/kg (NCA). Cycle life varies inversely with energy density (LFP achieves 3000+ cycles vs. 1000-1500 for NCA). Thermal runaway risk (i.e., uncontrolled exothermic reaction) remains a primary safety concern, mitigated through battery management systems (BMS) that monitor cell voltage, temperature, and state of charge (SOC). Cost has decreased by approximately 89% since 2010 (from $1,100/kWh to roughly $120/kWh), enabling broader market adoption.
